"Foul" describes something that is deeply unpleasant, offensive, or seriously wrong — whether to your senses, your moral values, or a set of rules. It's important to understand from the start that "foul" is not a mild word. It does not mean slightly bad or somewhat unpleasant. It carries a strong sense of genuine disgust, serious wrongness, or significant violation. Whenever you see "foul," expect the speaker to feel strongly about what they're describing.

1. Disgusting to the senses — especially smell and taste

This is the most common, everyday meaning of "foul." Something foul assaults your nose, your tongue, or sometimes your eyes. It provokes a feeling of revulsion — the kind that makes you want to step back or look away.

  • The garbage bin had been sitting in the sun all week. The smell was foul.
  • She took a sip of the old milk and immediately spat it out — the taste was foul.
  • The water in the pond looked dark and foul.
  • He opened the door to the abandoned house, and a foul odor rushed out.

Notice that "foul" here goes beyond just "bad-smelling." It implies something deeply offensive, almost unbearable. A foul smell isn't just unpleasant — it's the kind that makes your face scrunch up in disgust.

2. Dirty, filthy, or heavily polluted

"Foul" can describe something that is severely unclean, unhygienic, or contaminated. This sense often overlaps with sense 1, because heavily dirty things typically smell bad too. But the focus here is on the state of being dirty or polluted, not just the smell.

  • The prisoners were kept in foul conditions — no clean water, no sanitation.
  • The factory was dumping waste into the river, making the water foul.
  • The wound had not been cleaned and had turned foul.

3. Very bad weather or unpleasant conditions

When describing weather, "foul" means stormy, rough, bitterly cold, wet, or dark — the kind of weather that is genuinely harsh and miserable to be out in.

  • The sailors decided to stay in the harbor because of foul weather.
  • It was a foul night — cold rain, strong winds, and thick fog.
  • The hikers were caught in foul conditions on the mountain.

This sense can also stretch beyond weather to describe any conditions that are harsh, difficult, or unpleasant:

  • The team played the match in truly foul conditions (muddy field, heavy rain).

4. Morally offensive, wicked, or evil

Here, "foul" steps away from the physical and into the moral. Something foul in this sense violates basic standards of decency, ethics, or goodness. It describes acts, deeds, or words that are deeply wrong — not just mistaken or unkind, but genuinely offensive or evil.

  • The murder was a foul crime that shocked the entire city.
  • He was a corrupt official, known for his foul deeds.
  • The villain in the story committed foul acts against innocent people.

A very common expression connected to this sense is foul language — this means obscene, offensive, or vulgar words (swearing, profanity). It doesn't mean grammar mistakes or confused speech. It means words that are deliberately coarse and offensive.

  • The referee sent him off the field for using foul language.
  • She was shocked by the foul language in the film.

5. Against the rules; unfair or dishonest

In sports, "foul" describes a move or action that breaks the rules.

  • It was a foul tackle — he tripped the other player deliberately.
  • The referee stopped the game after the foul challenge.

More broadly, "foul" can mean achieved through dishonest, unfair, or criminal means:

  • He won the contract by foul means — bribery and deception.

This sense is also the foundation of the very important phrase foul play, which deserves special attention (see the phrases section below).

6. Blocked, clogged, or entangled (specialized/technical use)

This is a more specialized sense, used in technical, nautical (relating to ships and the sea), or mechanical contexts. Something foul in this sense is obstructed, tangled, or not working freely because something is in the way.

  • The pipe is foul — something is blocking it.
  • The anchor became foul (tangled in the anchor chain or caught on something underwater).
  • Foul ground (a nautical term for a part of the seabed that is dangerous for anchoring because it is rocky or cluttered with debris).

Unless you're reading older literature or something nautical or technical, you won't encounter this sense often — but it's good to recognize it.
Essential Phrases You Will Often See

Foul play
This is one of the most important and frequently used "foul" phrases. It has two related meanings:

  • In sports: breaking the rules deliberately, using unfair or illegal tactics.
    "The referee suspected foul play and stopped the game."*
  • In general life: dishonest, violent, or criminal activity — especially when someone is suspected of having been harmed or killed and it was made to look like an accident.
    "The detective didn't believe the man had died naturally. She suspected foul play."*
    "The investigation ruled out foul play — it was a genuine accident."*

When you hear "foul play" outside of sports, it almost always refers to this second meaning — that something suspicious, criminal, or violent has happened.

Foul mood
This is a very common informal phrase. A foul mood means an extremely bad, irritable, angry temper — someone who is in a foul mood is very difficult to be around, snapping at people, unhappy, and aggressive in their behaviour.

  • Don't bother him today — he's been in a foul mood all morning.
  • She came home in a foul mood after a terrible day at work.

Foul-mouthed
Describes a person who frequently uses foul language — someone whose everyday speech is full of offensive, obscene words.

  • He was a foul-mouthed character who offended everyone around him.

Fall foul of (something or someone)
This is a phrase meaning to get into trouble with, come into conflict with, or unknowingly break a rule or displease someone.

  • He fell foul of the tax authorities for not paying properly.
  • She fell foul of her boss after missing too many deadlines.
  • The company fell foul of new environmental regulations.

Notice that "fall foul of" can be used with people, organizations, rules, or laws. It doesn't mean a physical fall — it means to end up on the wrong side of something or someone.

By fair means or foul
This phrase means "using any method available, whether honest or dishonest, acceptable or not." It's used to describe someone who will do whatever it takes to achieve their goal, regardless of ethics.

  • He was determined to win the election by fair means or foul.

It's useful to understand where "foul" sits on the scale of similar words:

  • "Unpleasant" → mild, polite
  • "Nasty" → noticeably bad, stronger
  • "Disgusting" → very strong, causes real revulsion
  • "Foul" → similarly strong, but with an added sense of moral weight or deep violation — something that shouldn't exist, that crosses a line

"Foul" often implies not just that something is bad, but that it's wrong in a way that offends you deeply. It's the difference between saying "this soup tastes bad" and "this soup tastes foul" — the second suggests it is almost unbearable, genuinely revolting.
Register: When and Where Is "Foul" Used?

"Foul" is used comfortably in both formal and informal English.

In formal or literary writing, it often appears in phrases like "foul deeds," "foul murder," "foul play," or to describe weather and moral wrongdoing with a strong, serious tone.

In everyday informal speech, it can simply mean "very bad" or "disgusting":

  • "That was a foul meal." (I really hated it.)
  • "The traffic was absolutely foul today." (Terrible.)
  • "What a foul smell!"

In British informal English especially, "foul" is sometimes used as a strong general word for something truly unpleasant or terrible, even without a specific moral or physical element.

All these different meanings connect to a single idea: something that crosses a line — whether the line of cleanliness, the line of decency, the rules of a game, or the boundaries of acceptable behavior. "Foul" is always a strong word. It doesn't describe mild inconvenience. It describes something that genuinely offends, revolts, or seriously wrongs.

If you remember this — that "foul" means a strong, significant violation of some standard — you will be able to understand and use it correctly in almost every context you encounter it.
